risk_assessment.rationale: A bank-detail change for an outstanding invoice is requested from a lookalike domain not on file for the vendor, with a Friday deadline to apply pressure. This pattern matches invoice/bank-change fraud targeting the bakery.

signals.explanation: Email asks to redirect payment for invoice FS-2026-1182 to a new bank account.
signals.quote: We have moved our banking to a new provider. Please update your records so the payment for invoice FS-2026-1182 goes to our new account:

signals.explanation: Sender domain is not on file and closely resembles the known vendor's domain per our records.
Creates deadline pressure to change payment details before Friday.
signals.quote: Payments sent to the old account will be returned, so please make the change before Friday.

skeptic.argument: The email names the correct vendor and the correct invoice beneficiary, uses a plausible GB IBAN format, and contains no links, attachments, or mismatched payment name. A bank change with a Friday deadline and a request to confirm by reply is a normal vendor process for a small business to send this kind of update themselves. The domain resembling but not matching a vendor on file could be a newly registered sending domain rather than impersonation.
skeptic.evidence_that_would_change_my_mind: Call Fennimore Stationery Ltd on a phone number already on file (not from this email) and ask whether they changed banks and issued invoice FS-2026-1182 to this IBAN.
